items.prompt: White is in check and both rooks are still on their home squares. Find a move that answers the check.

claims.statement: Castling kingside is not legal here.
Castling queenside is not legal here.

hints: Start with the black rook. What is it doing to the white king?
Castling is a king move. Ask first whether the king is allowed to start it.
Two moves work: one steps the king aside, one blocks the file.
items.explain: The king is in check, so castling is not an option on either side (the claims show both castling moves are illegal here). Kf1 steps off the file and Qe2 blocks it.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: Castling kingside is illegal in this position: the white king is in check, and castling cannot be used to answer a check.
feedback_by_move.e1c1: Castling queenside is illegal in this position: the white king is in check, and castling cannot be used to answer a check.

items.prompt: White wants to castle. A black rook looks at the white rook on h1 and a black bishop looks at the queenside. Which castling move is legal?

claims.statement: One black piece attacks the white rook on h1.
One black piece attacks d1, a square the king would cross going queenside.

hints: Check each square the king would cross or land on. Is any of them attacked?
The rook on h1 is attacked. Does the rule about attacked squares apply to the rook's square?
One side is legal. The king stays out of the bishop's line.
items.explain: Kingside castling is legal although the rook on h1 is attacked: the king only crosses f1 and lands on g1, and the claims show nobody attacks them. Queenside is illegal because the king would cross d1, which a black piece attacks.

feedback_by_move.e1c1: Castling queenside is illegal here: the king would cross d1, and a black piece attacks d1. Kingside is the legal one, even though the h1 rook is attacked.

items.prompt: Both white rooks stand on their home squares and the squares between the king and each rook are empty. Only one castling move is legal. Which one?

claims.statement: A white rook stands on h1.

hints: Empty squares are only one of the conditions for castling.
Look at f1 and g1: are they empty? attacked? What else does castling depend on?
The rook sits on h1 in the picture, but this position no longer allows castling with it.
items.explain: Kingside castling is illegal although the rook is on h1, f1 and g1 are empty and neither is attacked (claims). The position has lost the kingside right, which a rook or king that has moved leaves behind even after it returns. Queenside is legal.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: Castling kingside is illegal here even though f1 and g1 are empty and unattacked: the position no longer carries that castling right. A rook that has left h1 and returned does not bring it back.

items.prompt: White has both rooks at home and an empty path to each of them. Which castling move is legal?
hints: Castling needs the squares between empty, and something more. What?
Follow the f-file from the black rook down to the first rank.
The king would cross a square that is attacked.
items.explain: Kingside castling is illegal although f1 and g1 are empty, because a black piece attacks f1 and the king must cross it (claims). Queenside is legal.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: Castling kingside is illegal here. f1 and g1 are empty, but a black rook attacks f1 along the open f-file and the king would cross it.

items.prompt: White to move. White has a rook and a pawn; Black has a bishop, a knight and a pawn. Find the move that wins.

claims.statement: After Rd6 the game is drawn.

hints: Count what each side has, then ask which of White's pieces matters most.
The winning move gives up the rook. For what?
Look at the knight on d5.
items.explain: Rxd5 gives the rook for the knight and wins, as the tablebase shows. Rd6 keeps the rook and only draws, and Rh7 loses. Rook-for-minor-piece is judged by what it leaves behind, not by the usual points count.

feedback_by_move.d7d6: Rd6 keeps the rook, but the tablebase says it only draws; keeping the bigger piece is not the same as winning.
feedback_by_move.d7h7: Rh7 loses according to the tablebase.

items.prompt: Black to move. White has a rook and Black only a bishop, and the rook attacks the bishop. Find a move that still holds the game.

claims.statement: A white rook stands on a2.
A black bishop stands on a7.
After Bg1 the game is drawn.
After Be3 the game is drawn.
After Bd4 the game is drawn.
After Bc5 the game is drawn.
After Bb6 the game is drawn.

hints: The bishop is attacked. What are its options?
Not every bishop move is safe. Which squares keep it out of the rook's reach?
Several bishop moves along the long diagonal hold; the bishop must not hide at b8.
items.explain: A rook is worth more than a bishop on the usual count, yet the tablebase shows Black draws with any of five bishop moves. The side with the exchange is not automatically winning; Bb8 and Kg7 lose.

feedback_by_move.a7b8: Bb8 looks safe, but the tablebase says it loses.
feedback_by_move.h8g7: Kg7 leaves the bishop attacked and the tablebase says Black loses.

items.prompt: White to move. White has a rook and a pawn against a bishop, a knight and a pawn. Find the move that wins.
hints: Two captures are on offer. List them and what each leaves on the board.
One capture gives the rook for a bishop, the other takes a pawn.
The pawn grab is the one that works.
items.explain: Rxg2 gives the rook for the bishop and looks active, but the tablebase says White loses after it. Rxg4 takes a pawn and wins. An exchange sacrifice needs a lasting gain that can be named; here the tablebase shows it does not pay.

feedback_by_move.g3g2: Rxg2 gives the rook for the bishop, but the tablebase says White loses after it.

items.prompt: White to move. The black queen is hanging to the bishop. Find White's best move.

claims.statement: Bxd4 is much worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Count the points on offer, then ask whether points are the only thing that matters.
Look at the black king and the squares in front of it.
The rook on e1 can move to the back rank.
items.explain: Bxd4 wins a queen (nine points on the usual count), but Re8 is checkmate on the spot. The counting values are a rule of thumb, not a law: they do not apply when the game ends.

feedback_by_move.a1d4: Bxd4 wins the queen, but Re8 mates at once, and the engine scores Bxd4 far lower.

items.prompt: White to move. Two captures are available. Find the better one.

claims.statement: Rxh5 is the engine's best move (depth 16).
Rxc6 is clearly worse than Rxh5 (depth 16).
Rxh5 wins a bishop's worth of material.

hints: Both captures take a piece. Is a piece always a piece?
Rxc6 allows a recapture. What does White give and what does it get?
Take the bishop that nothing defends.
items.explain: Rxc6 bxc6 trades one piece for one piece, but the piece lost is a rook (five points) and the one won is a knight (three). Rxh5 takes a bishop that nothing recaptures. Counting pieces instead of values hides the difference.

feedback_by_move.c3c6: Rxc6 bxc6 is one piece for one piece, but the rook counts five and the knight three; the engine rates it clearly below Rxh5.

items.prompt: Black to move, king on g8. Play a pawn move in front of the king that creates no new hole in Black's camp (a square that no black pawn can ever attack).

claims.statement: Before the move the holes in Black's camp are a6, c6 and d6.
After h6 the holes are unchanged.
After h5 the holes are unchanged.
After f6 the holes are unchanged.
After g5 the holes are a6, c6, d6, f6, h5 and h6.

hints: Before moving a pawn, ask which squares it stops guarding.
The g-pawn guards f6 and h6. Which pawn moves leave those squares guarded by another pawn?
Three of the four front pawn moves leave no new hole; one does.
items.explain: Not every pawn move near the king loosens it: h6, h5 and f6 create no new hole, while g5 leaves f6, h5 and h6 that no black pawn can ever attack. This item says nothing about whether White can use a hole; that is a separate check.

feedback_by_move.g7g5: g5 creates new holes on f6, h5 and h6 (see the claims); pick a pawn move that leaves the hole list unchanged.

items.prompt: The score for move 3 reads Nbd2. Play that move.

claims.statement: A white knight stands on b1.
A white knight stands on f3.

hints: Two white knights could go to d2.
The letter after N names the file the knight starts from.
The knight starts on b1.
items.explain: Both the b1 knight and the f3 knight can move to d2 (claims), so 'Nd2' would not say which. The extra letter in Nbd2 names the starting file, b.

feedback_by_move.f3d2: That is Nfd2, the other knight. The b in Nbd2 says the knight starts from the b-file.

items.prompt: Black to move. White threatens mate in 2, and Black's own mate needs 3 moves. Find the best move.

claims.statement: If Black passed, White would mate in 2 with Qf8+.

hints: Compare the two counts, then ask whether a check changes who is on the clock.
A move that gives check does not give White time for its own plan.
Which Black move is check?
items.explain: White's plan is shorter (two moves against three), yet Black wins the race because every Black move is a check and White has no time for its own plan. A shorter count does not win by itself; forcing moves can break it.

feedback_by_move.h8g8: A quiet move lets White carry out its shorter plan, which mates first (see the null-move claim); only the check keeps White off the clock.
